issues.legal_issue: Official land registers and the governing cantonment land regime can establish that land was held on an old-grant basis even when the original grant document is unavailable.
material_facts: The land was in a cantonment and the official general land registers recorded it as held on an old-grant basis by the recorded occupant.
The registers were old records maintained in the regular course under the applicable land-administration rules and came from proper custody.
The government’s file containing the grant was shown to have been stolen, and the claimants produced no document establishing title to the land or the nature of their predecessor’s rights.
The governing rules prescribed the terms of cantonment grants, including that the land remained government property.
issues.conclusion: The evidence established that the land was held on an old-grant basis; the High Court was not justified in finding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Regulation 6 of the Governor General in Council’s Order No. 179 of 1836 prescribed the conditions of cantonment land occupancy, including that the land remained government property and could not be sold by the grantee. The Cantonments Act, 1924, and the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1925, governed the administration and recording of cantonment land; Rules 3 to 5 provided for maintaining the general land register and mutation records. In Sh. Raj Singh v. Union of India, the Delhi High Court treated the 1836 Regulations as a self-contained scheme for grants and resumption, and this Court approved that decision in Union of India v. Tek Chand. The result differs from Union of India v. Purshotam Dass Tandon, where the government had not established its title or produced the grant and there was no supporting general land register. The changing descriptions of the claimants’ rights did not displace the official registers and governing regime.

rule.if: cantonment_land_title_suit and official_register_records_old_grant and register_kept_in_regular_course and (grant_document_unavailable or claimant_lacks_document_showing_land_title)

predicates.cantonment_land_title_suit: A claimant sought to establish title to land situated in a cantonment.
predicates.official_register_records_old_grant: The official land register recorded the land as held on an old-grant basis.
predicates.register_kept_in_regular_course: The land register was maintained in the regular course and came from proper custody.
predicates.grant_document_unavailable: The original grant document was unavailable to the authority responsible for the land records.
predicates.claimant_lacks_document_showing_land_tit: The claimant did not produce a document establishing title to the land or the nature of the predecessor’s rights.
predicates.old_grant_status_is_proved: The court finds that the land was held on an old-grant basis.

issues.definition: When a claimant disputes the status of cantonment land, a regularly maintained official register recording an old grant can establish that status where the original grant is unavailable or the claimant lacks a document showing title.

issues.legal_issue: An old-grant occupant does not own the government land, and a transfer of buildings or other property on it is subject to the required prior consent.
material_facts: The official registers and the governing land regime established that the land was held on an old-grant basis.
No conveyance of the land from the government to the recorded occupant or the occupant’s predecessor was produced.
The occupant’s heirs sold the property to the claimants without obtaining prior approval, and the claimants later sought a declaration of absolute ownership.
The applicable grant conditions retained government ownership of the land, allowed resumption, and restricted transfers of buildings to civilians.
issues.conclusion: The claimants did not establish ownership of the land; the land remained government property held under conditional occupancy rights, and the government was entitled to resume it in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Regulation 6 of the Governor General in Council’s Order No. 179 of 1836, cantonment land remained government property and could not be sold by the grantee; only buildings or other property on the land could be transferred, with the prescribed consent where the transferee did not belong to the army. The old-grant occupant was therefore in the position of an occupant or licensee, not the owner of the land. Sh. Raj Singh v. Union of India treated the grant as conferring revocable occupancy rights, and this Court approved that decision in Union of India v. Tek Chand.

rule.if: cantonment_land_title_claim and land_established_as_old_grant and no_government_conveyance_of_land and transfer_made_without_required_prior_consent

predicates.cantonment_land_title_claim: A claimant sought ownership of land situated in a cantonment.
predicates.land_established_as_old_grant: The court finds that the land was held under an old-grant arrangement.
predicates.no_government_conveyance_of_land: No document shows that the government conveyed ownership of the land to the occupant or a predecessor.
predicates.transfer_made_without_required_prior_con: The occupant or successor transferred property on the land without obtaining the required prior consent.
predicates.claimants_hold_only_conditional_occupanc: The claimants have no ownership of the land, hold only conditional occupancy rights, and the government may resume the land in accordance with law.

issues.definition: If a title claimant relies on an old-grant occupancy without a government conveyance, the claimant has only conditional occupancy rights, and an unapproved transfer does not prevent lawful resumption.

issues.legal_issue: A cantonment authority may direct construction to stop when the construction is considered an offence under the applicable building controls.
material_facts: The occupants were informed that prior permission was required for further construction.
The submitted building plans were rejected, but construction continued.
The authority issued a written notice directing that unauthorised construction stop, and the challenge to that notice was dismissed by the appellate authority.
issues.conclusion: The authority’s action in issuing the stop-construction notice could not be faulted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 185 of the Cantonments Act, 1924, authorised the Board to direct an owner, lessee, or occupier by written notice to stop the erection or re-erection of a building where the Board considered the work an offence under Section 184. The Board also had power to require alteration or demolition of an unauthorised structure.

predicates.challenge_to_cantonment_stop_constructio: A person challenged a written notice directing that building work in a cantonment stop.
predicates.required_permission_not_obtained: The person carrying out the building work had not obtained the required permission.
predicates.construction_continued_after_plans_were_: Building work continued after the submitted plans had been rejected.
predicates.authority_considered_work_a_building_con: The authority considered the building work an offence under the applicable building controls.
predicates.stop_construction_notice_is_valid: The authority’s direction to stop the building work is upheld.

issues.definition: When building work in a cantonment proceeds without required permission after plans are rejected, and the authority considers it an offence under building controls, a challenged stop-work notice is upheld.
